entities.summary: Pope Clement IX, born Giulio Rospigliosi, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 20 June 1667 to his death in December 1669. During his papacy, Clement IX played a key role in shaping the Catholic Church's response to the Thirty Years' War and its impact on European politics. He also oversaw the construction of several major churches and buildings in Rome, including the San Carlo all'Indice church, which was designed by his nephew, Francesco Borromini. Clement IX's papacy was marked by a significant increase in the number of new saints canonized during his reign, with over 300 saints being declared by him or his successors. This led to a renewed focus on the role of saints in Catholic devotion and practice. The papacy of Clement IX also saw the rise of the Jesuit Order, which played a significant role in the Church's missionary work and education. Clement IX's legacy continues to be felt in the Catholic Church today, with many of his papal bulls and decrees remaining in force. His death in 1669 marked the end of an era in the Church, as his successor, Pope Clement X, began a new period of reform and renewal. The papacy of Clement IX also had significant consequences for the Protestant Reformation, as his refusal to grant toleration to Protestants led to increased persecution and violence against Protestant communities in Europe.
